domanda: A user named User1 is assigned the Reader role at the scope of an Azure subscription named Sub1. User1 is also assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a resource group named RG1, which is in Sub1. RG1 contains a virtual machine named VM1. What are User1's effective permissions on VM1?
opzione_a: User1 can view VM1 but cannot modify it, because the Reader assignment at the broader scope takes precedence over the Contributor assignment.
opzione_b: User1 can create and manage VM1, but cannot assign roles on VM1.
opzione_c: User1 can create and manage VM1 and can assign roles on VM1.
opzione_d: User1 has no effective access to VM1, because the two role assignments conflict and cancel each other out.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): Azure RBAC is an additive model. As the Azure RBAC overview states, 'your effective permissions are the sum of your role assignments.' At the scope of RG1, User1 holds both Reader (inherited from Sub1) and Contributor (assigned directly), and the sum of those two is effectively Contributor. The Contributor role has Actions set to the wildcard '*', so it grants full management of VM1, but its NotActions include 'Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write' and 'Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete', which subtract the ability to create or delete role assignments. Therefore User1 can manage VM1 but cannot assign roles on it. (a) is wrong because it inverts the model: a role assignment at a broader scope never overrides or limits a role assignment at a narrower scope; RBAC has no concept of a more-specific assignment losing to a less-specific one, and nothing about Reader subtracts from Contributor. (c) is wrong because assigning roles requires 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write', which Contributor explicitly excludes via NotActions; a role such as Role Based Access Control Administrator, User Access Administrator, or Owner would be required. (d) is wrong because overlapping role assignments never cancel out or produce a conflict in Azure RBAC; only a deny assignment can block access that a role assignment grants.
tags: azure rbac,role assignment,effective permissions,additive model,contributor,reader,scope inheritance

domanda: A service principal named SP1 is assigned the Owner role at the scope of a resource group named RG-Prod. Azure has also applied a deny assignment at the scope of RG-Prod. The deny assignment specifies the '*/delete' action and applies to all principals, with no excluded principals. SP1 attempts to delete a storage account in RG-Prod. What is the result?
opzione_a: The delete operation succeeds, because a role assignment that grants the Owner role always takes precedence over a deny assignment.
opzione_b: The delete operation is blocked, because deny assignments are evaluated before role assignments and block access even when a role assignment grants it.
opzione_c: The delete operation succeeds, because deny assignments apply only to users and groups, not to service principals.
opzione_d: The delete operation is blocked only if SP1 also lacks the 'Microsoft.Authorization/denyAssignments/write' permission to remove the deny assignment first.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): Deny assignments take precedence over role assignments. Microsoft Learn defines a deny assignment as attaching 'a set of deny actions to a user, group, or service principal at a particular scope for the purpose of denying access' and states that deny assignments 'block users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access.' The documented evaluation sequence confirms the ordering: Azure Resource Manager retrieves all role assignments and deny assignments that apply to the resource, and 'if a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues' to the role assignments. Because the deny assignment covers '*/delete' and applies to all principals, SP1's Owner role does not help. (a) is wrong because it reverses the documented precedence; no built-in role, including Owner, overrides a deny assignment. (c) is wrong because the Principals property of a deny assignment accepts object IDs of users, groups, service principals, and managed identities, and the system-defined 'All Principals' principal represents every one of those object types in the directory. (d) is wrong on two counts: the block is unconditional, and deny assignments cannot be removed this way at all because currently all deny assignments have IsSystemProtected set to true, meaning they were created by Azure and cannot be edited or deleted.

domanda: Your organization is documenting how Azure evaluates access to resources. Which statements about Azure deny assignments are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Deny assignments are evaluated before role assignments, so a matching deny assignment blocks an action even when a role assignment grants that action.
opzione_b: An administrator who holds the Owner role at subscription scope can create a deny assignment directly from the Access control (IAM) page in the Azure portal.
opzione_c: A deny assignment can exempt specific security principals from the block by using the ExcludePrincipals property.
opzione_d: A deny assignment can be prevented from applying to child scopes by setting the DoNotApplyToChildScopes property to true.
opzione_e: Deny assignments and the NotActions property of a role definition are two names for the same enforcement mechanism.
spiegazione: Correct answers (a, c, d). (a) is true: the documented Azure RBAC evaluation sequence retrieves all role assignments and deny assignments that apply to the resource, and then 'if a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.' Deny assignments therefore short-circuit evaluation before any role assignment is considered. (c) is true: ExcludePrincipals is a documented deny assignment property holding 'an array of Microsoft Entra principal object IDs (user, group, service principal, or managed identity) to which the deny assignment does not apply.' It is commonly combined with the All Principals system-defined principal to deny everyone except a small set of accounts. (d) is true: DoNotApplyToChildScopes is a documented Boolean property that 'specifies whether the deny assignment applies to child scopes,' with a default value of false, meaning that by default a deny assignment is inherited by child scopes. Preventing inheritance to child scopes is listed in the docs as a capability of deny assignments that role assignments do not have. (b) is false: Microsoft Learn states explicitly, 'You can't directly create your own deny assignments. Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure.' They arise indirectly, for example from deny settings on a deployment stack or from Azure managed applications, and all deny assignments currently have IsSystemProtected set to true. No Azure role, including Owner, changes this. (e) is false: the docs contain a dedicated section titled 'Differences between NotActions and deny assignments' clarifying that they 'are not the same and serve different purposes.' NotActions is only a convenient way to subtract specific actions from a wildcard Actions entry within a single role definition, whereas a deny assignment is an actual block that overrides granted access.

domanda: Contoso creates an Azure custom role named VM Operator. In the role definition, Actions is set to 'Microsoft.Compute/*' and NotActions is set to 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete'. A user named User2 is assigned the VM Operator custom role at the scope of a resource group named RG-App. Separately, User2 is also assigned the Virtual Machine Contributor built-in role at the scope of RG-App. User2 attempts to delete a virtual machine in RG-App. What is the result, and why?
opzione_a: The deletion fails, because listing an action in NotActions creates an explicit deny for that action.
opzione_b: The deletion fails, because Azure subtracts the NotActions of every assigned role from the union of all Actions granted to the user.
opzione_c: The deletion succeeds, because Virtual Machine Contributor grants the delete action and NotActions is not a deny rule.
opzione_d: The deletion succeeds, but only after an administrator removes the VM Operator role assignment from User2.
spiegazione: Correct answer (c): NotActions is scoped to the role definition that contains it, not to the user. Microsoft Learn states this directly: 'If a user is assigned a role that excludes an action in NotActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same action, the user is allowed to perform that action. NotActions is not a deny rule - it is simply a convenient way to create a set of allowed actions when specific actions need to be excluded.' The subtraction 'Actions - NotActions = Effective control plane permissions' is computed per role definition; the results are then combined additively across the user's role assignments. The Virtual Machine Contributor built-in role includes 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete' in its Actions and has an empty NotActions, so the delete is granted and succeeds. (a) is wrong because it states the single most common misconception about NotActions; only a deny assignment produces an explicit deny in Azure RBAC. (b) is wrong because it describes an evaluation model Azure does not use: NotActions is never applied across role boundaries, so the VM Operator role's exclusion cannot reach into the Virtual Machine Contributor assignment. (d) is wrong because no removal is needed; the deletion already succeeds while both assignments are in place. To genuinely prevent the deletion, Contoso would need to remove the Virtual Machine Contributor assignment, since a wildcard-based custom role cannot subtract permissions that another role independently grants.
tags: azure rbac,notactions,custom role,virtual machine contributor,effective permissions,not a deny rule

domanda: An administrator named Admin1 is assigned the Owner role at the scope of an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 contains a storage account named sa1. Admin1 signs in to the Azure portal with their Microsoft Entra account, opens a blob container in sa1, sets the authentication method to Microsoft Entra User Account, and receives an authorization error when attempting to list the blobs. There are no deny assignments, locks, or network restrictions in place. What is the most likely explanation?
opzione_a: The Owner role definition lists the Microsoft.Storage resource provider in its NotActions.
opzione_b: The Owner role grants control plane access through a wildcard Actions entry, but the role definition contains no DataActions, so it does not grant access to blob data.
opzione_c: Owner role assignments made at subscription scope are not inherited by storage accounts in child resource groups.
opzione_d: Blob data access requires the role assignment to be made at the container scope; Azure ignores data access granted at subscription scope.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): Azure RBAC deliberately separates the control plane from the data plane. Control plane permissions come from Actions and NotActions; data plane permissions come from DataActions and NotDataActions. Microsoft Learn explains that this separation 'prevents roles with wildcards (*) from having unrestricted access to your data' and gives this exact scenario: a user with the Owner role at subscription scope has a wildcard action that inherits down and lets them perform all control plane actions such as reading, writing, and deleting containers, 'However, Alice cannot perform data plane actions without taking additional steps. For example, by default, Alice cannot read the blobs inside a container.' The Owner role has Actions set to '*' and no DataActions. The fix is to assign a role that includes blob DataActions, such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor, or to authenticate with the storage account access key instead. (a) is wrong because the Owner role's NotActions is empty; it is the absence of DataActions, not an exclusion, that causes this. (c) is wrong because role assignments are inherited by child scopes; the Owner assignment absolutely does reach sa1, which is why Admin1 can still see and manage the storage account resource itself. (d) is wrong because a role with blob DataActions works when assigned at subscription, resource group, storage account, or container scope; Azure does not ignore data access granted at higher scopes.
tags: azure rbac,dataactions,control plane,data plane,owner,storage blob data reader,troubleshooting

domanda: A user who is assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID reports that no Azure subscriptions appear on the Subscriptions page of the Azure portal, and that they cannot view the Access control (IAM) page for any management group. The tenant contains several active subscriptions. You must enable this user to regain access management over all subscriptions in the tenant. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the user the User Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID.
opzione_b: In Microsoft Entra ID, turn on the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to elevate the user's access.
opzione_c: Assign the user the Contributor role in Microsoft Entra ID under Roles and administrators.
opzione_d: Add the user as a Co-Administrator on each subscription.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): By default, Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles do not span both systems. Microsoft Learn states, 'by default, the Global Administrator doesn't have access to Azure resources.' The documented remedy is elevation: 'if a Global Administrator elevates their access by choosing the Access management for Azure resources switch in the Azure portal, the Global Administrator will be granted the User Access Administrator role (an Azure role) on all subscriptions for a particular tenant.' The docs note this 'switch can be helpful to regain access to a subscription,' which is exactly this scenario. As a best practice the elevation should be removed once the necessary role assignments have been made. (a) is wrong because User Administrator is another Microsoft Entra role that manages users and groups in the directory; it confers no permissions over Azure resources, so it reproduces the original problem. (c) is wrong because Contributor is an Azure role, not a Microsoft Entra role, and it cannot be assigned on the Roles and administrators page; Azure roles are assigned on the Access control (IAM) page of a management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. (d) is wrong because the classic subscription administrator roles, including Co-Administrator, are fully retired: they were retired and unsupported as of August 31, 2024, and as of May 2026 you must use Azure RBAC to manage access.
tags: microsoft entra id,global administrator,elevate access,user access administrator,azure roles vs entra roles,troubleshooting

domanda: User5 is assigned the Virtual Machine Contributor role at the scope of a resource group named RG-VMs. RG-VMs contains a virtual machine named VM1. User5 reports that an attempt to delete VM1 fails with an authorization error. Which of the following could explain the failure? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A CanNotDelete (Delete) management lock is applied to VM1 or is inherited from RG-VMs or the subscription.
opzione_b: A deny assignment that includes a matching delete action applies at the scope of VM1.
opzione_c: The Virtual Machine Contributor role definition does not include the 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete' action.
opzione_d: A different role that is also assigned to User5 lists 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete' in its NotActions, which subtracts the action from User5's effective permissions.
opzione_e: The role assignment was created only a few minutes ago, the change has not yet taken effect, and User5 has not signed out and signed back in.
spiegazione: Correct answers (a, b, e). (a) is a valid cause: management locks are independent of Azure RBAC. Microsoft Learn states that a lock 'overrides any user permissions' and that 'unlike with role-based access control (RBAC), you use management locks to apply a restriction across all users and roles.' CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource but cannot delete it, and locks are inherited, so a lock at RG-VMs or the subscription reaches VM1; the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. (b) is a valid cause: deny assignments 'block users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access,' and they are evaluated before role assignments. (e) is a valid cause: the docs note that 'when you assign roles or remove role assignments, it can take up to 10 minutes for changes to take effect,' that Azure Resource Manager caches configurations, and that signing out and signing back in forces a refresh of role assignment changes. (c) is false: Virtual Machine Contributor does include the virtual machine delete action. Its documented description is 'Lets you manage virtual machines, but not access to them, and not the virtual network or storage account they're connected to,' and managing virtual machines includes deleting them; the role's genuine gaps are the connected virtual network and storage account, and access to the data inside the VM. (d) is false because it repeats the classic NotActions misconception. Microsoft Learn is explicit that 'NotActions is not a deny rule' and that a user assigned a role excluding an action in NotActions who is also assigned a second role granting that action is allowed to perform it. NotActions is subtracted only within the role definition that declares it, so it can never remove an action that Virtual Machine Contributor grants.
tags: azure rbac,troubleshooting,resource lock,cannotdelete,deny assignment,notactions,virtual machine contributor,replication delay

domanda: User6 is assigned the Reader role at the scope of an Azure subscription named Sub1. User6 is also assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a resource group named RG1, which is in Sub1. Sub1 also contains a second resource group named RG2, on which User6 has no direct role assignment. A management lock with the CanNotDelete (Delete) lock level is applied to RG1. Select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented.
opzione_a: User6 can create a new storage account in RG1: [Yes | No]
opzione_b: User6 can delete an existing storage account in RG1: [Yes | No]
opzione_c: User6 can assign the Reader role to another user at the scope of RG1: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: User6 can delete an existing storage account in RG2: [Yes | No]
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: at RG1 the effective permissions are the sum of the inherited Reader assignment and the direct Contributor assignment, which equals Contributor. Contributor has Actions set to the wildcard '*', which permits creating resources. The CanNotDelete lock does not interfere, because the docs state that 'CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it' - create and modify remain allowed. Statement 2 - No: the CanNotDelete lock applied at RG1 is inherited by all resources in RG1, including resources added later, and the lock 'overrides any user permissions.' Locks apply across all users and roles regardless of RBAC, so Contributor does not help. Statement 3 - No: assigning a role requires the 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write' action. The Contributor role definition lists 'Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write' and 'Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete' in its NotActions, and effective permissions are computed as Actions minus NotActions, so this action is subtracted. Reader does not grant it either. User6 would need Role Based Access Control Administrator, User Access Administrator, or Owner. Statement 4 - No: the only assignment that reaches RG2 is the Reader role inherited from Sub1, which grants view-only access. The Contributor assignment is scoped to RG1 and is not inherited sideways to a sibling resource group, because scopes are structured in a parent-child relationship and only lower levels inherit from higher levels.

domanda: Your Microsoft Entra tenant contains a group named Group1 and a group named Group2. Group2 is a member of Group1. A user named User8 is a member of Group2. Group1 is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of an Azure subscription named Sub1, which contains a resource group named RG1. There are no deny assignments or management locks. Evaluate the following three statements: (1) User8 has Contributor permissions on Sub1, because role assignments are transitive for groups. (2) If User8 is additionally assigned the Reader role directly at the scope of RG1, User8's effective permissions on resources in RG1 are reduced to read-only. (3) If you assign User8 the Reader role directly at the scope of Sub1, the Contributor access that User8 receives through Group1 is removed.
opzione_a: User8 has Contributor permissions on Sub1, because role assignments are transitive for groups.
opzione_b: If User8 is additionally assigned the Reader role directly at the scope of RG1, User8's effective permissions on resources in RG1 are reduced to read-only.
opzione_c: If you assign User8 the Reader role directly at the scope of Sub1, the Contributor access that User8 receives through Group1 is removed.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: Microsoft Learn states that 'role assignments are transitive for groups, which means that if a user is a member of a group and that group is a member of another group that has a role assignment, the user has the permissions in the role assignment.' User8 is a member of Group2, Group2 is a member of Group1, and Group1 holds the Contributor role on Sub1, so User8 has Contributor permissions on Sub1. The token acquired for Azure Resource Manager 'includes the user's group memberships (including transitive group memberships).' Statement 2 - No: this is the classic misreading of the additive model. Azure RBAC computes effective permissions as the sum of all role assignments, so at RG1 User8 would hold Contributor (inherited from Sub1 via nested group membership) plus Reader (direct), and the sum is still Contributor. Adding a less privileged role never subtracts privileges; the Reader assignment simply has no impact. Only a deny assignment can block access that a role assignment grants. Statement 3 - No: for the same reason. Adding a Reader assignment does not remove or replace the Contributor access granted through Group1. To reduce User8's access you must remove the source of the Contributor permissions - for example, remove User8 from Group2, remove Group2 from Group1, or change the role assigned to Group1.

domanda: Case study: Fabrikam, Inc. uses a single Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains a resource group named RG-Finance. RG-Finance contains a storage account named safinance. A Microsoft Entra group named FinanceAdmins is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of Sub1. A user named User10 is a member of FinanceAdmins and is also assigned the Reader role directly at the scope of RG-Finance. A new business requirement states that User10 must be able to grant a colleague the Storage Blob Data Reader role on safinance. When User10 opens the Access control (IAM) page for safinance, the Add > Add role assignment option is disabled. You must resolve this while granting User10 the least privilege necessary. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign User10 the Owner role at the scope of RG-Finance.
opzione_b: Assign User10 the Role Based Access Control Administrator role at the scope of safinance.
opzione_c: Remove the Reader role assignment at the scope of RG-Finance, because it is overriding the Contributor permissions that User10 inherits from FinanceAdmins.
opzione_d: Assign User10 the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): The documented cause of a disabled Add role assignment option is that 'you're currently signed in with a user that doesn't have permission to assign roles at the selected scope,' and the documented solution is to be assigned a role that has the 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write' permission, 'such as Role Based Access Control Administrator, at the scope you're trying to assign the role.' User10's inherited Contributor role cannot assign roles because the Contributor role definition lists 'Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write' in its NotActions, and effective permissions are Actions minus NotActions. Role Based Access Control Administrator is described as letting you 'manage user access to Azure resources' and 'assign roles in Azure RBAC' without granting broad resource management, and assigning it at the storage account scope is the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement. (a) would technically work, because Owner has a wildcard Actions and no NotActions, but it grants full management of every resource in RG-Finance on top of role assignment rights, so it violates the least-privilege requirement stated in the scenario. (c) is wrong because it misstates how Azure RBAC combines assignments: the model is additive and the effective permissions are the sum of the role assignments, so a Reader assignment never overrides or suppresses an inherited Contributor assignment. Removing it changes nothing, and User10 would still be unable to assign roles. (d) is wrong because Microsoft Entra roles and Azure roles are separate systems; by default a Global Administrator has no access to Azure resources at all, so this neither addresses the problem directly nor respects least privilege.
tags: azure rbac,troubleshooting,role based access control administrator,contributor,notactions,least privilege,role assignment

domanda: A deployment stack protects a storage account named sa-stack. As a result, Azure created a deny assignment at the scope of sa-stack with the following configuration: Actions contains '*/delete'; Principals contains the All Principals system-defined principal; ExcludePrincipals contains the object ID of a user named User3; DoNotApplyToChildScopes is set to true. A user named User3 and a user named User4 are both assigned the Contributor role at the scope of the resource group that contains sa-stack. Which statement correctly describes the outcome?
opzione_a: Both User3 and User4 can delete sa-stack, because a Contributor role assignment at the resource group scope is inherited by sa-stack.
opzione_b: User3 can delete sa-stack, but User4 cannot.
opzione_c: Neither User3 nor User4 can delete sa-stack, because a deny assignment that uses All Principals applies to every principal in the directory regardless of any exclusions.
opzione_d: User4 can delete sa-stack, but User3 cannot, because ExcludePrincipals lists the principals that the deny assignment applies to.
spiegazione: Correct answer (b): The deny assignment blocks '*/delete' for the All Principals system-defined principal, which 'represents all users, groups, service principals, and managed identities in a Microsoft Entra directory.' Because deny assignments are evaluated before role assignments and block access 'even if a role assignment grants them access,' User4's Contributor role does not permit the deletion. However, ExcludePrincipals holds 'an array of Microsoft Entra principal object IDs ... to which the deny assignment does not apply,' and the docs note that 'All Principals can be combined with ExcludePrincipals to deny all principals except some users.' User3 is excluded, so the deny assignment does not apply to User3, evaluation continues to the role assignments, and User3's inherited Contributor role grants the delete. (a) is wrong because although the Contributor inheritance claim is true on its own, it ignores the deny assignment, which is evaluated first and blocks User4. (c) is wrong because it contradicts the documented purpose of ExcludePrincipals; the exclusion is honored, and combining All Principals with ExcludePrincipals is the standard documented pattern. (d) is wrong because it inverts the semantics of the two properties: Principals lists who the deny assignment applies to, and ExcludePrincipals lists who is exempt from it. Note that DoNotApplyToChildScopes set to true only stops the deny assignment from reaching child scopes such as blob containers; it has no bearing on sa-stack itself, which is the scope of the deny assignment.

domanda: Contoso defines an Azure custom role named Storage Ops with the following permissions block: Actions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/*'; NotActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete'; DataActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/*'; NotDataActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/delete'. A user named User7 is assigned the Storage Ops custom role at the scope of a storage account named sa2. User7 is also assigned the Storage Blob Data Contributor built-in role at the scope of sa2. User7 has no other role assignments, and no deny assignments or management locks exist. Select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented.
opzione_a: User7 can delete the storage account sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_b: User7 can delete a blob in a container in sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_c: User7 can read a blob in a container in sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: The effective control plane permissions of the Storage Ops role alone are computed as: [Actions minus NotActions | Actions plus NotActions | NotActions minus Actions]
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete' is subtracted from the Storage Ops wildcard by NotActions, and no other assigned role grants it. Storage Blob Data Contributor's Actions cover blob containers and the generateUserDelegationKey action, not deletion of the storage account resource itself. Because nothing grants the action, access is not allowed - not because NotActions denies it, but because no role grants it. Statement 2 - Yes: this is the key distinction. NotDataActions removed the blob delete action from the Storage Ops role, but the docs state that 'if a user is assigned a role that excludes a data action in NotDataActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same data action, the user is allowed to perform that data action. NotDataActions is not a deny rule.' Storage Blob Data Contributor includes 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/delete' in its DataActions, and RBAC is additive, so the deletion is allowed. Statement 3 - Yes: both roles grant the blob read data action; Storage Ops grants it through its blobs wildcard (blob read is not excluded by NotDataActions) and Storage Blob Data Contributor grants it explicitly. Statement 4 - Actions minus NotActions: Microsoft Learn defines the formula as 'Actions - NotActions = Effective control plane permissions', with the matching 'DataActions - NotDataActions = Effective data permissions' for the data plane. NotActions is never added to Actions, and the subtraction is never performed in the reverse direction; the subtraction is also computed per role definition, then the results of all of a user's role assignments are summed.
tags: azure rbac,custom role,notactions,notdataactions,dataactions,storage blob data contributor,effective permissions

domanda: A management group named MG1 contains an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 contains two resource groups named RG1 and RG2. A user named User9 is assigned the Owner role at the scope of MG1. An Azure managed application deployment caused Azure to create a deny assignment at the scope of RG1 with the following configuration: Actions contains '*/write'; Principals contains the All Principals system-defined principal; ExcludePrincipals is empty; DoNotApplyToChildScopes is set to false; IsSystemProtected is set to true. Evaluate the following three statements: (1) User9 can create a new virtual machine in RG1. (2) User9 can create a new virtual machine in RG2. (3) User9 can delete the deny assignment from RG1 by using the Azure portal.
opzione_a: User9 can create a new virtual machine in RG1.
opzione_b: User9 can create a new virtual machine in RG2.
opzione_c: User9 can delete the deny assignment from RG1 by using the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: creating a virtual machine requires write actions, which the deny assignment blocks via '*/write' for the All Principals system-defined principal with no exclusions. Deny assignments 'block users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access,' and in the documented evaluation sequence Azure Resource Manager checks deny assignments before role assignments: 'if a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.' User9's Owner role at MG1 is inherited down to RG1 but is irrelevant because evaluation never reaches the role assignments. Statement 2 - Yes: the deny assignment is scoped to RG1. Scopes are structured in a parent-child relationship, and inheritance flows only from parent to child, so a deny assignment at RG1 does not reach the sibling resource group RG2. Note that DoNotApplyToChildScopes is set to false here, which means the deny assignment is inherited by RG1's child scopes - but RG2 is not a child of RG1. User9's Owner role at MG1 is inherited by Sub1 and therefore by RG2, so the creation succeeds. Statement 3 - No: IsSystemProtected is set to true. Microsoft Learn defines this property as specifying 'whether this deny assignment was created by Azure and cannot be edited or deleted,' and notes that 'currently, all deny assignments are system protected.' The docs also state plainly that 'you can't directly create your own deny assignments. Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure.' No Azure role, including Owner, allows User9 to remove it; the correct approach is to remove the underlying managed application.
tags: azure rbac,deny assignment,management group,scope inheritance,owner,issystemprotected,managed application,all principals
